tagline: Across northern Nebraska, a two-lane byway links river bluffs and waterfalls.
intro: The Outlaw Trail follows Nebraska Highway 12 across northern Nebraska, with two lanes linking forested bluffs, grasslands, wetlands and river country. The Nebraska Department of Transportation lists it among the state’s scenic byways and gives its length as 231 miles, from Valentine to near South Sioux City. Visit Nebraska highlights waterfalls, winding rivers and high prairies along the journey. For much of its length, Highway 12 stays within ten miles of the South Dakota border.

Water has changed the communities along this corridor. Niobrara moved after a winter flood destroyed part of the original village in 1881, and the community later moved a second time. Farther east, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built Gavins Point Dam from 1952 to 1957, impounding the Missouri River as Lewis and Clark Lake.

East from Valentine, Highway 12 passes through Fort Niobrara National Wildlife Refuge toward Sparks, with a side trip to Smith Falls. Continue through Springview and Butte toward Monowi, then cross the Niobrara River into Niobrara. The road continues through the Santee Indian Reservation and Crofton, near Lewis and Clark Lake, then angles through Ponca. Ponca State Park lies north of town among steep, forested hills above the Missouri River. Highway 12 ends at U.S. 20 west of Jackson.

moments.title: Smith Falls
moments.text: Smith Falls drops 63 feet, the highest waterfall in Nebraska, on a spring-fed stream south of the Niobrara River. Its narrow canyon receives little direct sunlight and stays cooler than the surrounding landscape, sheltering paper birch and a hybrid grove of quaking and bigtooth aspen. Cool Niobrara canyons protected some boreal trees as the climate warmed after the ice age. Nebraska Game and Parks established the state park in 1992 through a lease with the Krzyzanowski family. The approach crosses a reused road bridge: the Verdigre bridge was reassembled here in 1996 as a 160-foot iron truss footbridge.
moments.notice: The footbridge over the Niobrara is a reused iron truss span.

moments.title: Monowi
moments.text: Monowi’s municipal road plan helps keep four streetlights funded. Elsie Eiler submits it as mayor of a village where she is the sole resident, as well as clerk, treasurer and librarian. The village lies between the Niobrara and Missouri rivers in eastern Boyd County. The 2000 census counted two residents, Elsie and her husband Rudy; his death in 2004 left her living alone in the village. Monowi had reached approximately 150 people in the 1930s before losing younger residents to growing cities with better employment prospects. Eiler maintains Rudy’s Library, approximately 5,000 volumes established in his memory.

moments.title: Ponca State Park
moments.text: High bluffs and steep wooded hills rise beside the Missouri National Recreational River at Ponca State Park. The park began in 1934 with a 160-acre donation sponsored by Ponca Legion Post 117; the Civilian Conservation Corps started developing the site that year. Eastern woodland flowers grow among prairie plants here, and Lewis and Clark’s expedition noted wild plum and gooseberry thickets while passing these bluffs in the summer of 1804. Bur oak, basswood, elm, black walnut and hackberry grow in the ravines and on the hillsides. The Three State Overlook gives a blufftop view into Nebraska, Iowa and South Dakota.
moments.notice: The Three State Overlook faces Nebraska, Iowa and South Dakota.
